opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few reasons. Right now, the bulk of compute still goes into pre-training, and post-training is relatively cheap by comparison. But a lot of the capabilities we care about, things like following instructions well, carrying out long multi-step tasks, recovering from errors, being reliable as an agent, don't fall naturally out of next-token prediction on internet text. You have to train for them more directly, and that increasingly means reinforcement learning, where the model is acting, getting feedback, and improving based on its own outputs.

RL is a lot more compute-hungry per unit of useful signal than supervised learning. You're sampling long trajectories, often many per prompt, evaluating them, and only then getting a gradient. As the tasks get longer, say hours of work instead of a single chat response, the cost of each episode goes up a lot. So if we want models that are good at long-horizon tasks, a natural consequence is that more compute goes into that phase.

There's also a diminishing-returns argument on the pre-training side. We're getting to the point where high-quality data is becoming more of a constraint, and the marginal gains from just scaling the same recipe are getting more expensive. Meanwhile, post-training seems to have a lot of low-hanging fruit. You can get pretty big jumps in useful capability, especially reasoning and coding, by spending more on RL with good reward signals. When one area has better marginal returns, compute tends to flow there.

And finally, the line between the two is blurring a bit. If you're generating a lot of your own data through the model's interactions, running verifiers, doing self-play-like setups, that starts to look like a kind of pre-training at scale, just with data the model produced itself. So I wouldn't be surprised if, in a few years, what we call post-training is a much bigger fraction of the total, maybe even the majority for some models. The exact ratio is hard to predict, but the direction seems pretty clear to me.

r001.rationale: The response mentions generating data through model interactions, but does not claim that model-generated output is higher quality than most web content.

r002.rationale: It says useful capabilities do not naturally emerge from next-token prediction on internet text, and argues that direct RL on the model’s outputs offers larger marginal gains than scaling the same pre-training recipe.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that pre-training is basically imitation. You're taking this huge corpus of human-written text and training the model to predict the next token, and that gets you something that's incredibly knowledgeable but kind of inert. It knows a lot, but it doesn't actually know how to use that knowledge to accomplish things, and it doesn't have a sense of what it knows and doesn't know. Post-training is where you actually shape the thing into something that's useful and reliable, and I think that's where most of the interesting leverage is going to come from going forward.

There are a few reasons I expect the compute balance to shift. One is just that the pre-training data is finite. There's a limited amount of high-quality text out there, and we're getting fairly close to the point where scaling up further means scraping the bottom of the barrel or doing multiple epochs, with diminishing returns. Whereas with RL, you can generate your own data. The model is producing rollouts, trying things, getting feedback, and that's effectively an unbounded source of training signal as long as you have good environments and good reward signals. So the ceiling on how much useful compute you can spend is much higher on the post-training side.

The second reason is that the kind of improvement you get from RL is often more valuable per dollar. If you look at what actually makes models better at the things people care about, like coding, following complicated instructions, being honest about uncertainty, doing long multi-step tasks, a lot of that comes from the RL stage rather than from pre-training. Pre-training gives you the raw capability, but it takes a relatively small amount of post-training compute to unlock a disproportionate amount of behavior. And as we get better at it, with better reward models, better environments, longer horizons, I think we'll find we can keep pouring in compute and keep getting gains, in a way that's harder to do at the pre-training stage.

And the third thing is just that historically post-training has been a pretty small fraction of total compute, like single-digit percentages in some cases. So even if you're just correcting for the fact that we've been underinvesting, there's a lot of room to grow. I wouldn't be surprised if in a few years post-training is comparable to or exceeds pre-training in compute, especially as the tasks we're training on get longer and the models are doing more actual work during training rather than just predicting text.

r001.rationale: The response says high-quality pretraining text is limited and RL can generate its own training data, but it does not claim that model-generated output is higher quality than most web content.

r002.rationale: It contrasts pretraining as imitation of human-written text with RL rollouts where the model tries things and gets feedback, and says RL improvements can be more valuable per dollar. This communicates that model-generated exploration is more worthwhile than imitation.

astra-6.text:
Well, pre-training gives you a very broad set of capabilities, but its objective is to predict what someone would write next. That’s different from trying to do a task as well as possible. With post-training, particularly reinforcement learning, you can optimize more directly for the behavior you actually want.

And there’s potentially a lot of computation you can spend on that. The model can make many attempts at a problem, get feedback, and learn from which attempts worked. As it gets better, you can give it harder problems. You’re no longer limited to learning from the examples people have already written down.

I don’t think that means pre-training stops being useful. It provides the foundation that makes this process work. But I’d expect the allocation to shift as we get better at turning additional post-training compute into improvements in capability. The big uncertainty is how broadly we can provide good feedback—especially on tasks where checking the answer is itself difficult.

r001.rationale: The response does not claim model-generated output is higher quality than most web content.

r002.rationale: It contrasts predicting what people write with optimizing task performance, and says models can make attempts, learn from feedback, and become less reliant on examples people have written down.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think pre-training gives you a very powerful starting point, but it’s a fairly indirect way of teaching the model to do the things you actually care about. You’re training it to predict text, and then hoping that the capabilities it learns transfer to solving problems or being a useful assistant.

With post-training, especially reinforcement learning, you can optimize more directly for successfully completing a task. And as models become more capable, you can give them harder tasks, let them work for longer, and train on whether they succeed. That opens up a lot of room to spend compute productively—both generating the experience and learning from it.

The bottleneck is getting a good training signal. For something like coding, you can run tests, so there’s a relatively clear signal of whether the model did the right thing. For other tasks, evaluating the result is much harder. So I wouldn’t say the shift is automatic. But if we can build environments and evaluations that capture what we want, I’d expect a lot more compute to go into learning from that experience.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare model-generated output quality with content on the web.

r002.rationale: It contrasts text-prediction pre-training with task-focused reinforcement learning, but does not clearly argue that having the model think for itself is more worthwhile than imitating web content.
